1 | INTRODUCTION

Competition between multi-sided platforms has sparked the interest of scholars and policymakers over the past decades (Rietveld & Schilling, 2020; Thatchenkery & Katila, 2022). These systems consist of a central firm—the platform owner—that connects complementors to consumers via an indirect network (Kretschmer et al., 2022). For example, app stores connect smartphone users to app developers, enabling transactions between them. Platforms exhibit strong economies of scale: a greater number of complementors increases consumer benefits through indirect network effects, resulting in a wider variety of complements (Rochet & Tirole, 2003, 2006). Platforms, therefore, rely on complementors for value creation (Agarwal et al., 2023; Loh & Kretschmer, 2023) and to successfully compete in the market (Shankar & Bayus, 2003). Consequently, scholars have studied owners' strategies to attract platform participants, such as pricing (e.g., Rochet & Tirole, 2003), exclusivity agreements (Cennamo & Santalo, 2013), or compatibility choices (Kretschmer & Claussen, 2016). Another stream discusses platform orchestration (and governance) as a determinant of market success, studying the rules and design features owners use to regulate and coordinate complementors' value creation (Claussen et al., 2013; Wareham et al., 2014).

However, we know less about the strategic choices made by complementors, despite their importance for platform-level outcomes. On the one hand, owners and complementors rely on each other for value creation (Jacobides et al., 2018). On the other hand, complementors are autonomous entities that pursue their own goals (Kretschmer et al., 2022), which may not always align with the owner's goals. While orchestration attempts aim to address such misalignment, complementors' agency remains a managerial challenge for platform owners. Put simply, complementors will only align their priorities with those of a platform only if it serves their own goals. This challenge is exacerbated by heterogeneity in complementor characteristics—such as market share or product-level network effects (Agarwal et al., 2023; Boudreau & Hagiu, 2009)—which increases the likelihood of diverging goals. Greater

heterogeneity implies more varied needs and expectations, making goal alignment more difficult to achieve. Therefore, our understanding of how complementor agency and heterogeneity shape their strategic choices vis-à-vis platform owners remains limited.

In this paper, we investigate how complementors' strategic choices are shaped by platform market competition. Complementors are affected by platform-level outcomes in ambiguous ways (Panico & Cennamo, 2022). While a growing platform increases indirect network benefits, it also intensifies within-ecosystem competition as other complementors join (Boudreau & Jeppesen, 2015). In addition, many platform markets are dominated by a single player (Biglaiser & Crémer, 2020; Shapiro & Varian, 1998), which extracts most of the co-created ecosystem value (Rietveld et al., 2020). Hence, platform growth presents a double-edged sword for complementors. In turn, platform growth is a function of the level of competition platforms face in the market. Yet, how between-platform competition affects complementor behavior is a largely open question.

Therefore, we examine how complementors respond when a new platform enters a market previously dominated by a powerful incumbent. Complementors are impacted in opposing ways: while the entrant threatens indirect network benefits by luring consumers away from the incumbent,1 it also constitutes an alternative with less intensive within-ecosystem competition. Complementors' reactions then depend on which of these “forces” dominates. This tension, however, is unlikely to resolve uniformly across heterogeneous complementor types. That is, some will primarily suffer from decreased network effects, while others will primarily benefit from a less competitive outside option in the entrant. To study the ambiguous implications for complementors' choices, we ask the following research questions: how does the entry of a rival platform affect (some of) the strategic choices complementors make? And how does this reaction differ across heterogeneous complementors?

We focus on two strategic choices: First, we investigate complementors' decision to multihome by joining the new platform. Before the entry, they had little choice but to affiliate only with the dominant incumbent. As multihoming is not costless (Cennamo et al., 2018), different complementor types will vary in their motivation to do so. Second, we study how the entry impacted complementors' responsiveness to one of the most salient incumbent's orchestration attempts. Specifically, we focus on complementors' willingness to participate in platform-wide sales, which are promotion periods aimed at coordinating collective discounts to create a concentrated period of high demand.2 Sales promotions are a prominent way for platform owners to orchestrate collective action among complementors and to facilitate joint value creation (cf. Chen et al., 2022). While these sales aim to generate a temporary increase in platform demand, their effectiveness depends on complementors' (voluntary) participation. However, for complementors, this involves a tension. By participating, they invest in the “collective good” (cf. Cennamo & Santalo, 2019) of high platform demand, benefiting themselves and others. At the same time, they forgo using discounts as a competitive action in the complement market—after all, they discount at the same time as their competitors. Hence, sales participation reflects how complementors balance their pursuit of collective and individual interests. Furthermore, this balance can shift in reaction to changes in the external environment (cf. Klein et al., 2019), for instance, in the competitive landscape in the platform market (Abolfathi, 2025;

Loh & Kretschmer, 2023). Sales promotions are also useful for studying this, as they constitute an orchestration tool subject to complementor participation that changes over time. Hence, studying complementors' repeated and dynamic choices regarding sales participation allows us to evaluate complementors' motivations to engage in collective action on a platform and how these are affected by changes in the level of between-platform competition. Lastly, we explore two dimensions of complementor heterogeneity, namely (i) their endowment with strategic resources and (ii) their reliance on network effects.

Empirically, we study the entry of Epic Games into the PC video game distribution market with the launch of its store in December 2018, which challenged the dominant position of incumbent platform Steam. This shift in the level of between-platform competition allows us to study the two strategic choices of interest for complementors in this setting, video game developers. That is, we investigate which complementor types were more likely to multihome by joining the Epic Games Store (EGS), and how the entry affected the rate at which they participated in Steam's platform-wide sales promotions, one of the incumbent's most prominent orchestration activities.

Our empirical results support our theoretical predictions. First, we find that complementors with weak strategic resources (independent developers) are more likely to multihome by joining the new platform. We attribute this to their struggle to prevail in the hyper-competitive incumbent ecosystem, which makes the prospect of less intense within-ecosystem competition on the entrant attractive. In contrast, complementors that are highly reliant on network effects (multiplayer developers) multihome at lower rates, as they depend on a unified consumer base on the incumbent. Second, we find that complementor heterogeneity drives variation in sales participation on the incumbent after the entry. Changes in between-platform competition shift how complementors balance their pursuit of collective and individual interests, leading to weakendowment complementors becoming less likely to participate in these sales after the entry, and those that are heavily reliant on network effects becoming more likely to do so. These findings contribute to the literature by showing how platform competition shapes complementors' strategic choices in nuanced and ambiguous ways, highlighting heterogeneity in their characteristics as a key determinant. We also discuss the implications of our findings for platform market entry and the effectiveness of platform orchestration.

2 | THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK AND HYPOTHESES

2.1 | Related literature

First, our paper connects to prior work on platform competition. Existing studies highlight how network effects shape platform adoption, market outcomes, and competitive strategies of platform owners (e.g., Cennamo & Santalo, 2013; Katz & Shapiro, 1985; Parker & van Alstyne, 2005). Yet, we know less about how such competition affects complementors. Recent work shows that the competitive standing of platforms influences complementors' activities and their value creation (Abolfathi, 2025; Loh & Kretschmer, 2023; Nagaraj & Piezunka, 2024; Thatchenkery & Katila, 2022), but it remains unclear how this translates into their strategic behavior. Second, we contribute to research on platform market entry. Network effects often create substantial incumbent advantages that deter entry (Biglaiser & Crémer, 2020), but entrants may succeed through higher quality, technological leapfrogging, or leveraging existing user bases (Eisenmann et al., 2011; Zhu & Iansiti, 2012). While prior studies have focused on

incumbents' reactions to the entry of a new platform (Casadesus-Masanell & Zhu, 2010; Seamans & Zhu, 2014), little is known about how complementors strategically respond. Third, our study links to the literature on multihoming, where complementors join multiple platforms. Multihoming increases competitive pressure and reduces platform profits (Landsman & Stremersch, 2011), yet the drivers of complementors' decisions to multihome remain underexplored. While prior work has studied different platform characteristics (Cennamo et al., 2018; Hagiu & Lee, 2011), we know less about how heterogeneity in complementor characteristics drives the choice to join multiple platforms. Finally, our work relates to studies of platform orchestration (or governance), which examine how platform owners align complementors' activities through regulation, incentives, or collective initiatives (e.g., Boudreau, 2012; Rietveld et al., 2021; Wareham et al., 2014). Closest to our study, Rietveld et al. (2020) show that greater dominance enables platform owners to exercise more exploitative governance. Still, we know little about what drives complementors' compliance with governance practices and how between-platform competition relates to complementors' motivation to engage in collective action within the ecosystem. Hence, it is a largely open question how between-platform competition shapes the effectiveness of orchestration strategies.

2.2 | Platform dominance and complementor heterogeneity

To analyze how an increase in between-platform competition affects the optimal strategic choices of complementors, we first discuss how a lack of platform-level competition impacts them. Platform dominance presents a double-edged sword for complementors (Panico & Cennamo, 2022). On the one hand, if consumer demand is concentrated in a single platform, complementors have access to the entire market there, maximizing indirect network effects (Shapiro & Varian, 1998). In contrast, if the consumer base is splintered across multiple platforms, the overall network benefit is diminished (Kretschmer, 2008).3 On the other hand, supply-side platform growth increases the within-ecosystem competition each complementor faces (Boudreau & Jeppesen, 2015), which also allows dominant platform owners to extract a larger share of the value created (Rietveld et al., 2020). Thus, while platform dominance offers the greatest potential for indirect network effects, the intensified within-ecosystem competition makes it difficult for complementors to capture these benefits fully.

This tension is unlikely to resolve uniformly across complementors with heterogeneous characteristics (cf. Boudreau & Hagiu, 2009). While some primarily benefit from the network effects of a unified consumer base, others are primarily hurt by the hyper-competitive landscape on dominant platforms. We propose two sources of complementor heterogeneity that shape how this tension resolves. First, complementors vary in their endowment with strategic resources. Technological and human resources enable the creation of innovative, high-quality products (Paladino, 2007), brand reputation drives market success (Deephouse, 2000), and financial resources support sustained consumer engagement (Kunz et al., 2017). Such resources are essential to attaining a competitive advantage (Barney, 1991) in the complement market, and thus condition how complementors experience the trade-off between network benefits and competition on dominant platforms. Those with weak resource endowments are less able to prevail in such hyper-competitive contexts and therefore more likely to suffer from platform

3Note that splintering can be an efficient outcome under some conditions, such as a high degree of consumer heterogeneity.

dominance. Second, complementors vary in their reliance on network effects. The returns to a larger consumer base vary, for example, when complement-level direct network effects are at play (Rietveld & Ploog, 2022). In this case, a larger demand side not only determines the potential market size, but it also directly affects the value of the complement to consumers.4 Therefore, a complementor that is reliant on network effects experiences greater marginal returns to demand-side platform growth than other types. On a dominant platform, they are therefore more likely to experience a net benefit in the tension between network effects and competitive pressure.

2.3 | Platform competition and strategic complementor choices

The dominance of an incumbent platform affects complementors in ambiguous ways. How, then, do they react when a new platform enters the market? Just as platform dominance presents a double-edged sword, so too does a challenge to it. On the one hand, the consumer base becomes splintered if some consumers move to the entrant. Because network effects arise from increasing returns to scale and the superadditivity of installed bases (Katz & Shapiro, 1994; Kretschmer, 2008), a splintered consumer base yields weaker network effects. Thus, the entry can harm complementors by undermining network benefits, even if they multihome across platforms. On the other hand, a new platform provides an alternative with less withinecosystem competition, as it initially hosts fewer other complementors (cf. Boudreau & Jeppesen, 2015). This gives complementors an opportunity to escape the incumbent's hypercompetitive landscape.

Consequently, the fate of complementors is closely tied to the structure of the platform market (Loh & Kretschmer, 2023; Nagaraj & Piezunka, 2024), and changes in its competitive landscape likely affect their strategic choices. While complementors make decisions across a wide range of variables, we focus on two. First, the entry of a rival platform lets complementors multihome. This expands market access by reaching consumers not affiliated with the incumbent (Belleflamme & Peitz, 2019), and complementors can partially escape the competitive pressure within the incumbent ecosystem. However, multihoming entails costs in compatibility investments (Cennamo et al., 2018), access fees (Armstrong, 2006), and added managerial effort across multiple customer bases. Complementors must weigh these costs and benefits when deciding whether to join the entrant. Given the ambiguous effects of between-platform competition, we expect heterogeneity in their multihoming decisions: those who are, on balance, harmed by the entry have less incentive to multihome, either because they benefit from a unified consumer base on the incumbent or because they can prevail in its competitive ecosystem. For others, the entrant is more likely to present an attractive outside option due to its less intense within-ecosystem competition.

Second, complementors' participation in platform-wide sales promotions is likely affected by the entry. These are limited periods during which the platform owner invites complementors to discount their products, creating a temporary surge in demand.5 However, pricing and

discounting decisions lie with complementors, so owners must orchestrate and incentivize sales participation. This reflects platform orchestration as a response to collective action problems (Chen et al., 2022), which arise from tensions between individual and collective interests (Bridoux & Stoelhorst, 2022). While complementors share a collective interest in high platformlevel demand (Cennamo & Santalo, 2019), they simultaneously compete for individual profits within the ecosystem (Boudreau & Jeppesen, 2015). Sales participation therefore represents a strategic trade-off: by participating, complementors invest in the collective interest of a high-demand period. At the same time, discounting their products in that way is not effective as a competitive action in the marketplace because they do so at the same time as their direct competitors.6 Hence, they forgo their individual interest in outperforming other complementors. Consequently, sales participation reflects complementors' relative pursuit of collective versus individual interests.

Two mechanisms tie the entry of a rival platform to complementors' subsequent sales participation. First, while a dominant platform can use its influence to align complementors with its orchestration practices (Rietveld et al., 2020), a challenge to its dominance may foster resistance to such “take-it-or-leave-it” governance (Uzunca et al., 2022). Second, depending on whether the entry is beneficial or detrimental, the balance between complementors' pursuit of individual and collective interests on the incumbent may shift. If they benefit from the entrant's less competitive environment, contributing to the collective goal of a growing incumbent ecosystem may no longer align with their individual interests, leading to less sales participation.7 Conversely, if complementors are primarily threatened by diminished network effects, they align more strongly with the collective interest of a growing and unified incumbent ecosystem, implying greater sales participation after entry. In sum, complementors' responses will vary with how they are affected by the entry.8

2.4 | Heterogeneous complementor reactions to the entry of a new platform

In the following section, we formulate hypotheses on how responses to the entry of the rival platform vary across different complementor types and the two strategic choices under investigation. We focus on complementors' endowment with strategic resources (Hypotheses 1a and 1b) and their reliance on network effects (Hypotheses 2a and 2b).

2.4.1 | The role of complementors' resource endowment

Firms' ability to compete in the marketplace stems from the presence of strategic resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable (Barney, 1991), such as a strong reputation

6Research on product discounts highlights important limitations related to discount frequency, including potential adverse effects on consumer price sensitivity and future sales (Alba et al., 1999; Kopalle et al., 1999; Marshall & Bee Leng, 2002). As a result, complementors have to consider the timing and frequency of discounts carefully. 7This can also be the case for those that do not currently multihome, but whose consideration to do so might already trigger a sales participation response. 8In our study, we analyze the two decisions separately. However, it is plausible that these choices are interdependent. We explore this conjecture in Appendices A (Additional analysis: Interdependence of decisions—Does sales participation determine multihoming?) and B (Additional analysis: Interdependence between decisions—Does multihoming determine sales participation?).

or brand, unique technological or managerial capabilities, or competent human resources (Helfat et al., 2023). We expect variation in resource endowment to influence complementors' reactions to the new platform's entry. For complementors that lack strategic resources, the detrimental effects of a hyper-competitive supply side outweigh the benefits of a greater demand side in the incumbent's ecosystem. Therefore, the entrant is an attractive alternative for this complementor type, due to its less intense within-ecosystem competition. Still, the entrant also hosts a smaller consumer side. Hence, complementors must evaluate both the absolute market size they encounter on the entrant and the share they are able to capture (Gans & Ryall, 2017). While all complementors face a smaller market size on the entrant, those with weaker resource endowment may find it more appealing due to reduced competition. The reason is that in highly crowded marketplaces, consumers cannot browse all available products (Dinerstein et al., 2018). This creates an issue for weak-endowment complementors more than for strong-endowment complementors, because the latter have ample resources to compete for attention (Meyer et al., 2024), regardless of the quality of their product. As a result, the prospect of joining the new platform creates the opportunity for weak-endowment complementors to gain greater attention there than they would in the crowded incumbent ecosystem. Although strong-endowment complementors can more easily afford the cost of joining the rival platform, they have much less to gain from it, as the potential gain in attention (and therefore in market share and performance there) is relatively lower than for weak-endowment types. As a result, the relative appeal of joining the entrant is expected to be greater for weak- than for strong-endowment complementors.9 In other words, the trade-off between a less competitive outside option and potentially diminished indirect network effects is more likely to resolve in favor of joining the entrant for complementors with a weaker resource endowment. As a result, we expect weak-endowment complementors to be more likely to multihome (by joining the entrant) than those with a strong endowment. Furthermore, weakendowment complementors should also become less likely to participate in sales after the entry, as their interests shift away from the pursuit of the collective interest and toward the pursuit of their individual profitability on the incumbent. We therefore hypothesize:

Hypothesis 1a. (Multihoming): Complementors with a weak endowment of strategic resources are more likely to join the entrant than those with a strong endowment.

Hypothesis 1b. (Sales participation): Complementors with a weak endowment of strategic resources are less likely to participate in the incumbent's platform-wide sales promotions after the entry of the rival, compared to those with a strong endowment.

2.4.2 | The role of complementors' reliance on network effects

Some complementors derive greater marginal returns from platform size than others (Rietveld & Ploog, 2022). In the case of complement-level network effects, a greater consumer side both provides indirect network benefits and directly determines a large part of a

9Note that this does not imply that only complementors with weaker resource endowment will perceive the entrant as attractive. Instead, the key point is that the relative attractiveness is greater for this type, which should result in systematic differences in the strength of their strategic responses.

complement's value to consumers (Agarwal et al., 2023; Ploog & Rietveld, 2025).10 We study the case where complement-level network effects do not operate across platform boundaries, which is common in several industries.11 For example, video game console providers typically prevent their users from playing multiplayer games with users of other consoles, which makes the complement-level direct network effect of multiplayer games platform-specific.12 In this case, the entrant is unattractive for complementors that are highly reliant on network effects: Not only does the entrant exhibit a smaller installed base of consumers, but it also threatens to splinter the network across multiple platforms. When the two platforms are not interoperable, this directly challenges the complement-level network effects, their value to consumers, and, in turn, the overall profitability of that type of complementor. Hence, this type is, in sum, more detrimentally affected by the entry, and they have less incentive to multihome by joining the entrant. After all, they are better off with a unified consumer base on the incumbent. At the same time, we expect this complementor type to become more likely to participate in sales on the incumbent after the entry. As they are highly reliant on a large consumer base, their individual interests are closely aligned with the collective interest of a greater and unified incumbent ecosystem. As the entry threatens to splinter the consumer base, we expect the interests of complementors that are highly reliant on network effects to shift even further toward alignment with the collective interest. Accordingly, we hypothesize:

Hypothesis 2a. (Multihoming): Complementors that are highly reliant on network effects are less likely to join the entrant than those that are less reliant on network effects.

Hypothesis 2b. (Sales participation): Complementors that are highly reliant on network effects are more likely to participate in the incumbent's platform-wide sales promotions after the entry of the rival, compared to those that are less reliant on network effects.

3 | SETTING AND DATA

3.1 | Institutional background

We empirically study the predictions from our theoretical framework in the context of the PC video game distribution market, where the dominant incumbent platform, Steam, was challenged

10Such a high reliance on network effects adds another dimension to the incumbency advantage in platform markets. This advantage stems from the incumbent's larger consumer base relative to the entrant (Biglaiser et al., 2019) and constitutes a significant barrier to entry. As a result, attracting complementors can be challenging for the entrant (Zhu & Iansiti, 2012). This is particularly true for complementors that rely on complement-level network effects and when platforms are not interoperable. 11In some cases, complement-level network effects are not platform-specific, and our arguments do not necessarily apply to them. For example, network effects among users of messaging apps such as WhatsApp operate across different mobile operating systems. In addition, recent years saw the emergence of “cross-play” functionality in the video game industry. In Appendix D (How the “cross-play” functionality could affect our study), we briefly discuss this development and explain why it does not pose a concern for our study. 12Similar dynamics apply to user reviews: more reviews generate informational benefits and thus app-level direct network effects, but only within the platform where they appear—for example, iPhone users see only App Store reviews, Android users only Google Play reviews. Other examples of platform-specific complement-level network effects include Netflix or Prime Video watch parties, ride-sharing options on Uber or Lyft, and data-driven improvements to recommendations.

by the entry of a powerful competitor, the Epic Games Store. Video games are typically developed for one or several technology platforms such as the PC (22% of global market value in 202213), smartphones and tablets (49%), or game consoles (29%).14 In this paper, we focus on PC games. Initially sold in physical format, they are now mostly downloaded from online stores or played online.15 The value chain comprises several key players, including game developers, publishers, hardware manufacturers, engine developers, and retailers. Game developers vary widely in size, ranging from large studios producing “Triple-A” games to smaller, independent ones, commonly referred to as “Indie” developers. While large developers were predominant in the early stages of the industry, digitization enabled the entry of many smaller players, resulting in an increased quantity and variety of products available in the market (Waldfogel, 2019).

The PC video game industry and Steam: Digital games are distributed through online platforms, which may be owned by publishers themselves (e.g., Ubisoft or EA's stores) or operated as marketplaces that host both first-party and third-party games, such as Steam and the Epic Games Store (EGS). Since its launch in 2003, Steam, owned by the American firm Valve, has remained the leader in the distribution of digital games, with about 130 million monthly active users in 2023, as shown in Figure 1a.16 It offers a large variety of games from all genres, including both single- and multiplayer titles, from independent to large publishers such as Activision Blizzard or Microsoft. While a few games are first-party games,17 most of the games offered on Steam are from third-party developers. These developers retain control over their product pricing, while the platform charges a transaction-based fee per sale.

Orchestration activities: In our setting, both Steam and EGS engage in a variety of orchestration activities aimed at shaping the behavior of users and complementors. For example, both platforms enforce content moderation policies for games and user reviews, and Steam operates an anti-cheating system to maintain a fair multiplayer environment. In terms of incentives, both Steam and EGS rely on a standard per-transaction fee model.18 One particularly important orchestration activity is the organization of sales, in which the platform invites developers to offer discounts on their games to stimulate demand temporarily. These sales typically last around 2 weeks, attract significant attention, and stimulate demand for games and the platform as a whole, in particular during the Winter and Summer sales.19

One might worry that EGS's launch expanded the market by attracting entirely new consumers, but this seems unlikely for two reasons. First, EGS's catalog and features were not distinct enough from Steam's to draw a new audience, unlike Nintendo's Wii, which reached new demographics through novel gameplay. Second, both platforms exhibit similar post-launch growth patterns, and Figures C7 and C8 show no decline in Steam's active user base. Hence, any expansion effect from EGS does not seem to compromise our analysis. 17That is, games developed or published by the platform owner, such as Half Life or Counter Strike. 18Steam also provides orchestration through infrastructure and community features. It offers an API for developers, facilitating integration with the platform, and hosts a range of community-driven programs such as Trading Cards, the Steam Workshop, and Early Access that promote user engagement and interaction. These features enhance the platform's value proposition but also serve as strategic tools to encourage continued participation by both consumers and complementors. Steam also developed many features that foster the discovery of new products through a powerful recommendation system and consumer engagement through a review system. For a detailed discussion of these orchestration mechanisms, see Rietveld et al. We focus on sales participation as it provides a particularly informative lens on complementor responses to platform orchestration. Sales events are among the platform's most salient orchestration activities,20 and participation in them represents a recurring, observable, and time-varying decision at the publisher or developer level, making it ideally suited for empirical analysis.21 We argue that participation in platform-wide sales reflects complementors' willingness to align with the platform's orchestration efforts and their engagement in sustaining the broader health of the ecosystem.

Competitive landscape: Even though other digital stores were launched after Steam,22 they are operated by major publishers, primarily distributing their own products. Access for thirdparty developers is typically limited, leaving few viable alternatives for independent and smaller developers to reach consumers. As a result, Steam maintained a dominant position in the PC game distribution market. By 2018, its market share was estimated to range between 50% and 70% (Wu & Zhang, 2019), confirming its position as the market leader. With about 26,000 games available at that time, the number of games offered on Steam has continued to grow steadily, reaching over 71,000 games at the end of 2023,23 with more than 8000 new games released each year since 2018.24

In December 2018, Epic Games launched the Epic Games Store, a digital marketplace offering services similar to those of Steam. In addition to distributing third-party games, EGS also features a small number of first-party games, most notably the highly successful Fortnite. Despite a smaller initial user base, EGS quickly drew developer interest due to its favorable 12% revenue-share model. To expand its consumer and developer bases, Epic pursued two key strategies. It secured exclusivity agreements with major titles (e.g., Tom Clancy's The Division 2 in 2019)25 and attracted users by offering a free game each week. Leveraging its ownership of the Unreal Engine (a widely used 3D computer graphics tool), Epic also stimulated adoption by waiving the engine's royalty fee for games sold through EGS, alongside its more generous revenue-sharing model (Wu & Zhang, 2019).

By the end of 2023, the Epic Game Store averaged over 75 million monthly active users, as shown in Figure 1a, and its catalog was approaching 3000 games. While Steam remains the largest player, EGS has established itself as a viable alternative, showing steady growth in both its consumer base and the number of affiliated complementors.26

Steam's reaction to Epic's entry: When facing the entry of a rival platform, an incumbent has several strategic tools at its disposal to mitigate competitive pressure and preserve the integrity of its established ecosystem. One such tool is pricing: the incumbent may adjust its revenuesharing model by lowering transaction fees or introducing a tiered pricing structure that favors some complementors—particularly those generating substantial demand. In addition to pricing, incumbents may respond by securing (additional) exclusivity agreements or expanding their in-

20Other key orchestration activities involve introducing social and community-oriented features. 21Another orchestration mechanism, studied in prior work (Rietveld et al., 2019, 2021), is the selective promotion of complementors, where platforms stimulate demand for certain complementors or complements through badges, quality seals, or paid placements. Steam, however, does not offer paid promotion. See https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/ marketing/visibility/. Instead, it relies on algorithmic visibility driven by popularity and quality metrics, preventing complementors from “buying” exposure. 22For example, Microsoft Store in 2005, Ubisoft's Uplay in 2012, and EA Origin in 2013. 23https://gamalytic.com/blog/steam-revenue-infographic. 24https://steamdb.info/stats/releases/. 25Some remained available through publishers' own channels, such as Ubisoft Connect, or on consoles. 26See Figures C7 and C8 in Appendix C for more details on the evolution of the number of users on Steam.

In November 2018, shortly before the launch of the Epic Games Store, Steam announced a shift to a tiered revenue-sharing model that offered more favorable terms to topselling games.27 This strategy likely reflects an attempt to retain high-performing complementors in anticipation of increased platform competition.28

3.2 | Data collection

We collected game characteristics and prices via web scraping and merged datasets using Steam's unique game identifiers or, when unavailable, fuzzy name matching.29 The total sample consists of 11,439 games, of which 9335 are only observed on Steam, 1458 only on EGS, and 645 on both platforms as of June 2022. First, we retrieved data on 12,460 games and their characteristics available on Steam using the platform's API. We obtained a wide range of game characteristics, namely their genres (e.g., “Action,” “Strategy,” “Adventure”), Steam store categories (e.g., “Multi-Player,” “Steam Cloud”), as well as the names of their developers and publishers.30 We also obtained information on the technical characteristics of games, as well as their dates of release on the platform. We also collected consumer reviews, including reviewer details, timing, and sentiment (positive or negative). In the absence of sales data, the number of reviews serves as a proxy for game performance on Steam. Finally, we collected daily prices for these games from Steamdb.info, covering the period from January 2015 to June 2022.31 We were able to obtain this information for 10,746 games. We collected prices and discounts in US Dollars. In addition, and crucial for parts of our empirical analysis, this data source also contains information on game discounts offered as part of Steam-wide sales promotions. This allows us to systematically track each game's participation in these events. We complemented our data with player activity from Steamcharts. com,32 which provides time-varying player numbers—monthly before 2020 and daily thereafter—for about 13,350 titles. Our scrape, completed in January 2022, thus captures the most popular Steam games at that time.

Second, we directly collected data from the Epic Game Store, covering all 1706 games available at the time. For each game, we retrieved its release date on the platform, along with a set of game characteristics that are broadly comparable to those observed on Steam.

4 | EMPIRICAL FRAMEWORK

We expect that platform entry influences complementors' strategies—some are more likely to multihome or engage in sales promotions than others. This section outlines how we operationalize these constructs and describes our empirical strategy.

4.1 | Variables

4.1.1 | Outcomes of interest

We analyze two strategic choices made by complementors. First, we analyze the determinants of multihoming, that is, their decision to join the entrant's platform in addition to the incumbent's. To test our first set of hypotheses, we use a binary dependent variable indicating whether a game became available on EGS after its launch. Second, we analyze how complementors' responsiveness to the incumbent's orchestration attempts changes after EGS's launch by studying their participation in Steam's sales promotions (i.e., Steam sales).34 We argue that participation in these sales promotions reflects complementors' willingness to engage in collective action on the incumbent by making an investment into the “public good” of platform growth (Cennamo & Santalo, 2019). As such, we interpret complementors' participation in these events as indicative of the balance they strike between the pursuit of individual interests and alignment with collective goals.35

4.1.2 | Heterogeneous complementor types

In our hypotheses, we formulate expectations about how different types of complementors respond to the entry of a rival platform. In particular, we highlight the role of their resource

33See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Unreal_Engine_games. 34As explained above, these promotional periods semi-regularly take place on the platform. Steam invites, but does not force, game developers to participate in these sales by discounting their games for a certain duration. 35As also noted earlier, developers also pursue individual objectives when discounting their games. However, during platform-wide sales, they coordinate the timing of discounts with others, limiting their use as a competitive tool. To further support our interpretation of sales participation as a response to orchestrated collective action, we conduct a mechanism test in Appendix B (Additional analysis: Discounts outside sales). Specifically, we find no change in discounting behavior outside promotional periods following the entrant's launch, suggesting that complementors adjust their behavior only in response to the incumbent's orchestration efforts, which is consistent with a shift in the balance between individual and collective interests.

Page 15

endowment and reliance on network effects. Empirically, we classify game developers into distinct types that capture these dimensions.

Strong vs. weak resource endowment (Hypotheses 1a and 1b): Similar to the movie and music industries, video game producers can be roughly divided into major (“Triple-A”) and independent (“Indie”).36 The most salient differentiating factor between the two is their endowment with resources, financial and others. Triple-A games are produced with substantially larger development budgets, which are expected to exceed 1 billion US Dollars in the near future (Zollner, 2023). These resources enable the formation of large development teams,37 investments in cutting-edge technologies to produce high-fidelity games, and the development of inhouse marketing capabilities that support highly effective promotional efforts. In contrast, indie games—while not a clearly defined term—are commonly associated with “simple gameplay, simple graphics, small teams” (Dutton, 2012). In addition, Triple-A developers operate large legal departments, allowing them to engage in direct negotiations with platform owners such as Steam. This grants them considerable “persuasive resources” (Ryall, 2013) as well. Accordingly, we capture variation in resource endowment via the distinction between Triple-A and Indie developers. We therefore test our first hypothesis using a binary variable that identifies games developed by Indie developers, representing complementors with weak resource endowment.

High vs. low reliance on network effects (Hypotheses 2a and 2b): Some games offer functionalities that allow consumers to play together online. These multiplayer games are subject to complement-level network effects (Rietveld & Ploog, 2022), which makes them more reliant on a large, unsplintered consumer base.38 Without such a unified network, multiplayer games are unable to fully realize their value potential. This is in contrast to singleplayer games, which are played individually and therefore exhibit less dependence on a large consumer base. Accordingly, we capture reliance on network effects using a binary variable indicating multiplayer games.

4.2 | Empirical approach: Multihoming analysis

In this part of our analysis, the dependent variable is a binary indicator of multihoming, defined as a game's affiliation with the entrant's platform (EGS) by the end of our observation period— approximately 3 years after the entry took place. We expect the probability of multihoming to be higher for Indie than non-Indie games (Hypothesis 1a) and lower for multiplayer than singleplayer games (Hypothesis 2a).

Sample: Because we are interested in how the incumbent's complementors respond to the entry of a rival, we restrict our analysis to games available exclusively on Steam or on both Steam and EGS, excluding those available only on EGS. We also excluded games developed by Valve, the firm that owns and operates Steam. We define multihoming as the decision by a developer to make a game available on EGS at any point between December 2018 (the launch of EGS) and June 2022 (when data collection concluded). Our final sample, for which all

That is, consumers can only play games together using the same platform. Please see our additional discussion in Appendix D (How the “cross-play” functionality could affect our study).

Regression model and identification: We estimate a logit model in which the dependent variable takes the value of one if game i has also joined EGS by June 2022, and zero otherwise. A value of zero can be interpreted as the developer's decision to remain exclusive to Steam, despite EGS having been available for over 3 years. Importantly, joining EGS is a one-off decision for each game, resulting in no within-unit variation over time. As such, we have to resort to a cross-sectional analysis. This approach introduces the challenge that games are not randomly assigned to the types we are interested in (that is, Indie and multiplayer). These types are likely to be correlated with other structural attributes that also influence multihoming decisions, raising concerns about endogeneity due to an omitted variable bias. To address this concern, we implement a combination of strategies, including control variables, fixed effects, and matching techniques, as detailed below. We model the decision to multihome as follows:

Multihomingi = α + β1 × Indie + β2 × Multiplayer + β3Xi + γg +γr + ϵi:

Multihomingi is a binary variable coded as one if the game is available on both platforms and zero otherwise. The terms Indie and Multiplayer are binary indicators capturing the game types relevant to our hypotheses. The main coefficients of interest are β1 and β2, which correspond to Hypotheses 1a and 2a, respectively. We also include two sets of fixed effects and a range of controls to address the aforementioned endogeneity concerns. First, we include genre fixed effects, denoted by γg, to account for variation in competitive intensity across market segments.40 Second, we also include release year fixed effects, denoted γr, to capture life cycle dynamics.41

The vector Xi includes a set of control variables designed to account for potential lock-in effects and other factors that might influence a developer's multihoming decision. To capture experience on the incumbent platform, we include the number of games previously released on Steam by both the developer and the publisher. In addition, Steam offers a range of standardized features that developers can incorporate into their games,42 which can further “tie” the game to the platform. For each of these features, we include a binary indicator of whether the game utilizes it. In contrast, the availability of games on home consoles may indicate a lower degree of platform-specific lock-in. We, therefore, include a dummy indicating whether the game was released on any major console. We also include a dummy variable indicating whether a game was developed with Epic's Unreal Engine. Since Epic offers preferential revenue-sharing terms on EGS for such titles, using the engine may provide an additional incentive to multihome.

Finally, we include a set of variables to proxy for a game's quality and popularity. Here, we control for its price (a higher price may indicate higher quality and possibly higher demand),

4.3 | Empirical approach: Sales participation analysis

In Hypotheses 1b and 2b, we make predictions about how the launch of the EGS affects complementors' participation in the incumbent's sales promotions. We expect the probability of participation to decrease for Indie games (weak resource endowment, Hypothesis 1b) and increase for multiplayer games (high reliance on network effects, Hypothesis 2b). We test our hypotheses within a difference-in-difference (DiD) framework. Throughout, the dependent variable is a binary indicator equal to one if game i participated in a Steam sale s, and zero otherwise. We, therefore, estimate how the probability of sales participation differs between the periods before and after the launch of EGS, and how this change varies across different game types.

Sample: In our main specification, we restrict the sample to a 2-year window, that is, 1 year before and 1 year after the launch of EGS, in order to account for seasonal effects. During this period, Steam held 27 sales events.46 Some were highly specialized while others were broader, leading to wide variation in participation rates (ranging 0.13%–75.17%). To focus on the main events, we include only sales with at least 1% of games participating in our main specification.47

This leaves us with a total of 18 Steam sales, out of which seven took place in the year before EGS's launch and 11 afterwards. Furthermore, since we are interested in how complementors' incentives to participate in orchestration activities evolve, we restrict the sample to the 4191 games already available on Steam at the start of the observation period. Then, the unit of observation in our regressions is a game–sale; that is, we observe each game during the period of each sale in our sample and evaluate whether it participated in that sale. Our final regression sample consists of 75,179 game–sale observations.

Regression model and identification: We face several empirical challenges. First, to test our hypotheses, we use two different “treatment” indicators in our DiD framework: Indie and multiplayer games. Therefore, we face empirical challenges because we estimate differences across game types that may not be comparable in terms of their tendency to participate in Steam sales.48 Such differences may also affect their ability to optimally react to EGS's launch. We control for such differences in two ways: (i) we include game fixed effects throughout to account

A second challenge arises from heterogeneity across different Steam sales. As noted above, some target broader sets of games than others. In addition, the platform determines both the timing and the nature of sales events, which may be driven by strategic considerations. Most importantly, the launch of the EGS may have prompted the organization of additional sales to keep consumers on the incumbent.49 We account for these potential confounding factors by including sale fixed effects (e.g., “Winter Sale 2018”) throughout our analysis. That is, our estimates can be understood as the probability of a game participating in a sale, conditional on the nature of the sale itself, which is unobserved by us. This approach also accounts for games' average tendency to participate in a sale, which is likely a function of how many sales take place within a certain time period. In our setting, Steam organized more sales after EGS's launch, which may have made game developers more selective about which ones to participate in. Together, we estimate econometric models of the following form:

Y is = α + βi Afters × Ti ð Þ + βXXis + γi + γs + ϵis:

Here, Y is is our dependent variable, a binary indicator equal to one if game i participated in sale s, and zero otherwise. After s indicates sales that took place after the launch of EGS, and Ti is our “treatment” indicator for a specific game type. In addition to fixed effects, we also include a vector of four time-varying game-level control variables, denoted Xis. First, we control for the total number of Steam reviews a game has received by the time of a sale, using this as a proxy for its prior market performance in the absence of direct sales data. Second, we control for the share of positive “thumbs up” reviews to capture differences in perceived game quality. Third, we control for a game's age (in days) to capture unobserved differences in their tendency to participate in sales, which may vary over their life cycle. Fourth, we include the number of games in the same genre available on Steam, reflecting the level of within-ecosystem competition a game faces based on its market positioning.50 Next, γi and γs are game and sale fixed effects. Note that the latter also controls for unobserved time trends.51

Lastly, we run part of our analysis on matched samples.52 Specifically, we use coarsened exact matching (CEM) based on the control variables in Xis, but measured at the time of EGS's launch.53 Therefore, we only compare (i) Indie to non-Indie and (ii) multiplayer to singleplayer that exhibit similar performance, audience reception, age, and intra-platform competition.54

Finally, for the sample of games released before EGS's launch, we observe an average of 3240 user reviews per game, with 78% of them being positive.

We focus our discussion on Model 5, which includes the complete set of controls and fixed effects. First, we find strong support for Hypothesis 1a: Indie games are 2.98 percentage points (SE = 0.0072) more likely to multihome than non-Indie games. This result is consistent with the idea that Indie developers are more inclined to shift their value creation to the entrant's ecosystem, which is, at least initially, less competitive. Given the sample mean of 7.06% of multihoming games, this is also an economically sizable effect. Second, we also find support for Hypothesis 2a. The estimated coefficient for multiplayer games is negative and statistically significant in most specifications, suggesting that these games are less likely to multihome compared to singleplayer ones. This may indicate the presence of dynamic effects. To explore this possibility, we conducted an additional analysis focusing on the timing of multihoming (see Appendix A, Additional analysis: Timing of multihoming).

5.1.3 | Additional analyses

We conducted a series of additional analyses to test the robustness and underlying mechanisms of our main results. Appendix A contains the full details. First, we analyze the timing of multihoming using hazard models based on release dates across platforms (Appendix A, Additional descriptive statistics: Timing of multihoming and Additional analysis: Timing of multihoming). Consistent with our main results, indie games are more likely to multihome and do so more quickly than major games. In addition, multiplayer games are less likely to multihome and do so less quickly than singleplayer games. Second, to examine the role of switching costs, we split the sample by release date relative to EGS's entry (Appendix A, Additional analysis: Games released before and after the EGS launch). Results are consistent with our main findings. Third, we investigate whether multihoming depends on game quality and popularity (Appendix A, Additional analysis: Pre-EGS quality and popularity of games). While higher user ratings (quality) are positively related to multihoming for all game types, the number of ratings (popularity) matters most for indie games. While consistent with our theoretical arguments, this adds nuance to our main findings, and we discuss this in greater detail in the appendix. Fourth, we also explore whether developers' decisions to multihome depend not only on individual game characteristics but also on their interaction. Results from the interaction model suggest a nuanced pattern: the effect of being an indie game remains strongly positive and significant when the game is not multiplayer, but the combination of indie and multiplayer characteristics yields a smaller and statistically insignificant effect. This suggests that the effect of the indie characteristics on multihoming is “attenuated” when the game also offers multiplayer features (Appendix A, Additional analysis: Interaction between games characteristics). Fifth, we examine whether multihoming is related to greater sales participation before the entry, that is, whether the two decisions are interrelated (Appendix A, Additional analysis: Interdependence of decisions—Does sales participation determine multihoming?). We found no evidence to support that conjecture. Sixth, we explore variation in within-ecosystem competition as a potential determinant of multihoming (Appendix A, Additional analysis: Multihoming and within-genre competition). As the competitive landscapes (based on genres) are very similar across the two platforms, we do not find evidence for an effect. Lastly, we provide additional robustness tests by using coarsened exact matching (Appendix A, Robustness check: Coarsened exact matching)

5.2 | Sales participation analysis

5.2.1 | Descriptive statistics

Table 3 presents descriptive statistics for our main sample. On average, 38% of games participate in sales. Additionally, sales increase in the period following the launch of EGS compared to before. In fact, as illustrated in Figure 1b, Steam increased the number of sales per year between 2017 and 2020. This may be a reaction to the launch of EGS, and we address this issue by including sale-fixed effects throughout.

Next, 49% of our games in the sample were developed by Indie developers, resulting in a roughly even split for this treatment group, and 36% offer multiplayer functionality. In terms of time-varying control variables, games have an average of 4130 reviews at the time of a sale, and 77% are positive. Moreover, the average game is 1518 days old.61 Furthermore, the average game faces competition from 1639 others in the same genre within Steam.62

5.2.2 | Main results

The main results of our sale participation analysis are presented in Table 4. Throughout, we estimate linear probability models, as they allow for two-way fixed effects and let us include and interpret interaction terms in a straightforward manner. Standard errors are clustered at the game level. In Hypothesis 1b, we hypothesized that complementors with a weak resource endowment are less likely to participate in sales after EGS's launch than those with a strong endowment. We test this hypothesis in Models 1, 3, and 4, and we find consistent support. In Model 1, which uses the full sample without matching and only includes the DiD term interacted with the Indie game indicator, we find that the probability of sale participation is 1.4 percentage points (SE = 0.0048) lower for Indie games after EGS's launch, compared to non-Indie games. In Model 3, we run a full model, including the DiD terms involving the multiplayer indicator. We still find support for Hypothesis 1b, albeit with a slightly smaller coefficient (β = −0.0117) that is estimated with slightly lower precision (SE = 0.0048). Finally, in Model 4, instead of using time-varying controls, we estimate our model using a matched sample.63

That is, each Indie game is only compared to non-Indie games of similar performance, audience reception, age, and facing similar intra-competition. Such a match is found in only 3021 games, reducing the sample size. Still, Hypothesis 1b is again supported with an even larger estimated effect size: Indie games are 2.04 percentage points less likely to participate in Steam sales after EGS's launch, compared to non-Indie games (SE = 0.0067).

Next, in Hypothesis 2b, we hypothesized that complementors that are highly reliant on network effects are more likely to participate in sales after EGS's launch. We test this in Model 2, using the full sample and including only the DiD term with the multiplayer game indicator. We find support for the hypothesis: Multiplayer games participate in sales with 2.58 percentage points higher probability (SE = 0.0049) after EGS's launch, compared to singleplayer games. We estimate effects of similar magnitude and statistical precision when estimating the full model (Model 3, β = 0.0246, SE = 0.0050), and when using a matched sample (Model 5, β = 0.0254, SE = 0.0068). Together, we find support for Hypotheses 1b and 2b. While the effects we estimate are statistically significant, they are relatively small in size. On average, games in our sample participate in 38% of sales. Based on our most conservative estimates obtained with matched samples, the probability of participation is 2.04 percentage points lower for Indie as compared to non-Indie games, and 2.54 percentage points higher for multi- than singleplayer games. Hence, our results suggest that complementors' reactions, in terms of their participation in sales promotions, are relatively mild.

5.2.3 | Additional analyses

We ran additional analyses to explore the robustness of our findings on sales participation and the underlying mechanisms. Detailed results are provided in Appendix B. First, we distinguish between major and minor sales, based on the number of participating games (Appendix B, Additional analysis: Minor versus major sales). We find that effects are driven by minor sales, which suggests that complementors continue participating in high-visibility sales but become more selective in engaging with smaller-scale sales. Second, we analyze how the entry affected discounting outside Steam's sales promotions (Appendix B, Additional analysis: Discounts outside sales), and do not find any effects. Hence, we are confident in interpreting our main results as a reaction in terms of complementors' responsiveness to orchestration attempts.64 Third, we explore the possible interaction between our focal complementor characteristics (i.e., Indie and multiplayer), which are not mutually exclusive and may give rise to conflicting predictions (Appendix B, Additional analysis: Interaction between games characteristics). Our results suggest that no “type” dominates the other. Fourth, we examine if post-entry sales participation is determined by multihoming, that is, if the two choices are interrelated (Appendix B, Additional analysis: Interdependence between decisions—Does multihoming determine sales participation?). We do not find any evidence to support this claim. Finally, we show that games with higher pre-EGS popularity (review count) and quality (review score) are more likely to participate in sales after the entry (Appendix B, Additional analysis: The role of pre-EGS review count and score). While this adds nuance to our main findings, we consider it fully consistent with our theoretical arguments.

64We conducted additional analyses to assess the impact of the entry on prices across different complementor types in Appendix C (Additional analysis: Impact of the entry on prices). Here, we do not find any impact of games' current prices (i.e., discounted or undiscounted). However, we do find a significant change in list prices (i.e., undiscounted). Indie games tended to increase their prices after the entry (in particular those that multihome), while multiplayer games tended to decrease them. This may indicate that developers use these prices to steer demand across platforms in ways that are consistent with our theoretical arguments.

6 | DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION

We investigate how the level of between-platform competition shapes complementors' strategic choices. Specifically, we examine how the entry of a powerful rival platform challenged an incumbent's dominance and influenced (i) complementors' decision to multihome by joining the rival, and (ii) their participation in the incumbent's platform-wide sales promotions— reflecting their responsiveness to orchestration attempts and willingness to engage in collective action within the incumbent's ecosystem. The entry of a rival platform affects the motivations behind these choices in ambiguous and heterogeneous ways. On the one hand, it threatens the network benefits complementors derive on the incumbent, reducing their profitability. On the other hand, it offers an opportunity to escape the intense within-ecosystem competition on the incumbent. How this tension resolves determines complementors' multihoming and sales participation decisions. However, because complementors differ in their needs and characteristics, the resolution is not uniform: some are primarily harmed by diminished network benefits, whereas others mainly benefit from an alternative for value creation with less within-ecosystem competition. We develop and test hypotheses about how different types of complementors respond to entry, focusing on two sources of heterogeneity: their endowment with strategic resources and their reliance on network effects.

Empirically, we study our research questions in the PC video game distribution market, where the dominant incumbent platform, Steam, faced the entry of a powerful rival, the Epic Games Store. We find broad support for our hypotheses: For complementors with weaker resource endowment (Indie developers), the opportunity of a less competitive alternative outweighed the potential loss in indirect network effects. They therefore became more likely to multihome by joining the entrant and less likely to participate in the incumbent's sales promotions, indicating reduced responsiveness to its orchestration attempts. Conversely, complementors that are highly reliant on network effects (multiplayer developers) are primarily threatened by diminished network benefits. Consequently, they were less likely to multihome and became more likely to participate in the incumbent's sales promotions.65

6.1 | Implications

Our findings have several implications for both platform owners and complementors. First, the level of platform competition is a key determinant of complementors' strategic choices. This is due to the complex and often ambiguous interdependencies between platforms and their complementors. While platform owners' success relies on the support of complementors, the reverse is less straightforward: Not all complementors benefit equally from platform success because the tensions between network effects and within-ecosystem competition do not resolve uniformly across heterogeneous complementors. As a result, complementors differ in their profitmaximizing strategies, such as platform affiliation and compliance with orchestration.

Second, our findings have implications for firms seeking to enter platform markets. The well-known “chicken-and-egg” problem (Caillaud & Jullien, 2003) limits initial network

65Further analyses highlight that complementors' responses to a rival platform's entry depend on the interaction between their resource endowment and reliance on network effects. See the results presented in Appendices A (Additional analysis: Interaction between games characteristics) and B (Additional analysis: Interaction between games characteristics).

benefits and hinders the adoption of new platforms by complementors and consumers. Yet, our findings suggest that entrants can use a “divide-and-conquer” strategy that targets specific types of complementors early on. In particular, complementors with a weak resource endowment are more likely to join the entrant, as they benefit from reduced within-platform competition. At the same time, this implies that new platforms would initially attract a peculiar set of complementors, which may be of lower value individually and contribute to the platform's niche character. This also implies challenges for incumbents. While network effects generally raise entry barriers, they may not be sufficient to deter all threats, as increasing within-ecosystem competition can drive some complementors to seek alternatives. This finding adds nuance to the value of “incumbency advantage” in platform markets (Biglaiser & Crémer, 2016).

Finally, our findings also contribute to policy discussions around platform dominance. The heterogeneous reactions of complementors to the entry highlight that their welfare is tied to the platform-level market structure in complex and ambiguous ways. Consequently, antitrust remedies aimed at “breaking up” large platforms may not yield uniform benefits for all complementors. In particular, those relying on unified consumer bases would be adversely affected. As such, regulatory interventions should account for the diversity of complementor interests and the trade-offs they face in platform environments.

6.2 | Contributions

We make several contributions to the platform literature. First, prior studies on platform competition have focused on strategic choices made by platform owners (e.g., Cennamo & Santalo, 2013; Jin & Rysman, 2015; Seamans & Zhu, 2014; Seamans & Zhu, 2017), but only a little attention has been paid to the choices made by complementors—a crucial determinant of platforms' competitive performance. Our contribution lies in analyzing how the platform-level market structure affects complementors' strategic choices, thereby advancing our understanding of their role in driving and responding to between-platform competition.

Second, we contribute by showing that heterogeneity in complementor characteristics leads to variation in their likelihood to multihome. Prior literature has generally been limited in its exploration of the determinants of multihoming, with only a few studies analyzing platformlevel factors (Cennamo et al., 2018; Hagiu & Lee, 2011). We expand this perspective by highlighting complementor-level factors. Our findings also inform a broader discussion on the relationship between multihoming and platform competition (e.g., Armstrong, 2006; Landsman & Stremersch, 2011)—differences in complementors' incentives to multihome determine their prevalence, which in turn determines the intensity of competition across platforms.

Third, we highlight how complementor-level factors can determine successful entry into platform markets. While prior studies have focused on platform-level attributes and strategies (e.g., Seamans & Zhu, 2014; Zhu & Iansiti, 2012), our paper shows how complementor characteristics (resource endowment and reliance on network effects) shape their incentives to support a new platform. Thus, we contribute to the literature by showing how heterogeneity among complementors influences the dynamics of platform market entry.

Finally, our study contributes to the literature on platform orchestration (or governance). Prior work has emphasized how platform owners design and implement governance mechanisms. Still, it has largely overlooked the agency of complementors in complying with governance attempts (Abou-El Komboz et al., 2023). We contribute by highlighting that successful governance is determined not only by the actions of platform owners but also by the

This also complements prior research explaining how platform dominance influences governance practices by owners (Rietveld et al., 2020). Hence, we contribute by showing that market structure is a critical determinant of the effectiveness of platform orchestration.

6.3 | Limitations and future research

Our study also has several limitations. First, we only study reactions to the entry of the EGS by complementors on Steam, the largest and most prominent platform in the PC video game distribution market, but not other platforms.66 Our focus is justified by data availability (on Steam) and by the fact that Epic's entry constitutes a particularly salient market shift. Still, future research should provide a more comprehensive analysis of how cross-platform competitive dynamics shape complementor strategies. Second, we focus on two specific strategic choices made by complementors. However, they make a broader set of strategic choices (e.g., pricing and positioning) that are also likely to respond to platform competition and offer promising avenues for future research. Third, for our study of product-level network effects, it is important to note that we study a context where the two platforms are not interoperable on the consumer side. This means that network effects do not operate across platforms. However, in other settings, this can differ, namely when competing platforms are interoperable and complementlevel network effects extend across platforms.67 The mechanisms described in our paper might not hold in such cases, and complementors' strategic responses to platform market entry may differ. Studying a case without interoperability thus constitutes a clear boundary of our work, and we leave it to future research. Finally, our empirical setting exhibits some peculiarities that may limit the generalizability of our results. We therefore encourage future research to replicate and extend our approach in a broader range of empirical settings.

APPENDIX A: ADDITIONAL ANALYSES ON THE MULTIHOMING DECISION

This appendix presents additional descriptive statistics and regression results that both demonstrate the robustness of our main findings and provide further insights into the mechanisms driving complementors’ multihoming decisions.

A.1 | Additional descriptive statistics: Timing of multihoming

Our multihoming analysis is based on a cross-section of games for which we construct a binary indicator: it takes the value one if a game appears in both catalogs (Steam and Epic) at the end of the observation period, and zero otherwise. For a subsample of games, we observe the exact release dates—on Steam for singlehoming games and on both platforms for multihoming games. For this subsample, we compute the number of weeks between the two release dates (if multihoming occurs). We use this duration as an alternative dependent variable to assess how our key characteristics influence the timing of multihoming, including both games that multihome and those that remain exclusive to one platform.

occurs—if it occurs. This censored duration, illustrated in Figure A1, serves as the dependent variable in additional analyses. The aim is to estimate the influence of our key characteristics (Indie and multiplayer) on the likelihood and timing of multihoming, including both games that eventually multihome and those that remain exclusive. This approach allows us to incorporate some dynamic aspects into the analysis.

More precisely, we estimate a series of duration models using both semi-parametric and fully parametric specifications, relying on the same variables as in our main models. The dependent variable is a continuous measure of the number of weeks until multihoming, if it occurs. This variable is available for 8026 games, as reported in Table A1. Our estimation sample includes games that never multihomed (93.7%), games released on Steam before joining Epic (3.97%), and games released simultaneously on both platforms (1.71%). We exclude the 48 games that were first released on EGS and then on Steam, as well as 84 games for which time-varying control variables are missing, resulting in a final cross-sectional sample of 7846 games.

From this sample, we construct a panel dataset that begins with the entry of EGS in December 2018. Games remain in the panel until they multihome, resulting in repeated observations with both time-varying and time-invariant controls. The final panel comprises 1,123,805 weekly observations, with 429 events (i.e., games multihoming) observed. We estimate a set of proportional hazard (PH) and accelerated failure-time (AFT) models. These models enable us to assess the effect of our two key variables of interest—Indie and multiplayer—on the time to multihoming and the likelihood of remaining exclusive (i.e., survival without multihoming).

We present our estimation results in Table A2. In the Proportional Hazard (PH) models, a coefficient greater than 1 implies that an increase in the corresponding regressor raises the hazard rate, that is, increases the likelihood of multihoming. In contrast, the interpretation is reversed in Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) models: coefficients above 1 indicate a longer expected survival time—in our context, a lower likelihood or slower timing of multihoming. The results are broadly consistent across model specifications, although some differences in sign and significance levels appear. To assess model suitability, we first perform a Schoenfeld residuals test, which rejects the proportional hazards assumption. We therefore place greater emphasis on the AFT models. Among these, the specification using a log-normal hazard distribution (Column 6) provides the best fit based on the AIC criterion. Focusing on this preferred specification, we find that the exponentiated coefficient for the Indie indicator is 0.994 (p < .001), indicating that Indie games are more likely to multihome and tend to do so sooner, supporting Hypothesis 1a. The exponentiated coefficient for the Multiplayer indicator is 1.003 and significant at the 10% level, suggesting that multiplayer games are slightly less likely to multihome and multihome at a slower rate, supporting Hypothesis 2a. Overall, the survival analysis provides further support for both Hypotheses 1a and 2a, reinforcing our interpretation of complementor behavior in response to the platform's entry.

A.3 | Additional analysis: Games released before and after the EGS launch

Using our main specification, we explore some of the underlying mechanisms by splitting the sample into games released before and after the launch of EGS. This distinction is potentially meaningful: games released before EGS had the opportunity to generate sales on Steam and may have become subject to lock-in effects. For these games, multihoming implies splitting an existing player base and potentially incurring switching costs. In contrast, games released after

Across both subsamples, Indie games are consistently more likely to multihome, supporting our main findings. A.4 | Additional analysis: Pre-EGS quality and popularity of games

We further examine the role of game popularity and quality in shaping complementors’ decisions to multihome. Focusing again on the subsample of games released before the EGS launch, we investigate how two measures of market performance on Steam—the number of reviews and the share of positive reviews—relate to the multihoming decision, and how these relationships vary across different types of games. To this end, Table A4 presents results from a series of sample splits: between Indie and non-Indie games (Models 1 and 2), and between multiplayer and singleplayer games (Models 3 and 4). Across nearly all specifications, we find that a higher share of positive reviews is associated with a greater likelihood of multihoming. expecting to generate additional revenue from the new platform. In contrast, the review count—which we interpret as a proxy for prior sales—exhibits a more nuanced pattern. We find a positive association only for Indie games. This aligns with our theoretical expectations: Indie developers, facing more intense competition on Steam, are more likely to perceive EGS as an attractive outside option. They multihome with their higher-demand titles to exploit new revenue opportunities. For multiplayer games, however, we do not observe a similar pattern. This is consistent with our theoretical framework: The types of complementors that are most likely to multihome are even more likely to do so with their most popular and well-received titles, which likely promise the highest marginal returns from expanding market access over multiple platforms.

A.5 | Additional analysis: Interaction between games characteristics

Table A5 explores whether developers’ decisions to multihome depend not only on individual game characteristics, but also on their interaction. In Column 2, we introduce interaction terms to capture how the combination of being an indie and a multiplayer game may jointly influence multihoming behavior. Results from the interaction model suggest a nuanced pattern: the effect of being an indie game remains strongly positive and significant when the game is not multiplayer, but the combination of indie and multiplayer characteristics yields a smaller and statistically insignificant effect. This suggests that the positive association between the indie characteristics and multihoming is “attenuated” when the game also offers multiplayer features.
