A.6 | Additional analysis: Interdependence of decisions—does sales participation determine multihoming?

We examine whether the two strategic choices under study—multihoming and participation in sales promotions—are interdependent. We test whether complementors that participate in more sales are also more likely to multihome. To do so, we restrict the analysis to the sample of games used in the sales participation analysis, that is, those that were already active on Steam prior to EGS's launch. Model 1 in Table A6 reports results for this restricted sample and confirms the robustness of our main findings. In Model 2, we include a variable capturing the total number of sales in which a game has participated. The coefficient is not statistically significant, suggesting no clear relationship. In Model 3, we differentiate between sales participation before and after the launch of EGS to allow for potential dynamics. Again, both coefficients are statistically insignificant. Taken together, these results do not support the notion that sales participation and multihoming are interdependent strategic choices.

A.7 | Additional analysis: Multihoming and within-genre competition

This set of analyses aims to assess how the relative attractiveness of platforms—particularly in terms of within-genre competitive intensity—affects the likelihood that complementors choose to multihome. To conduct this exercise, we construct a monthly-level catalog of games on each platform (Steam and Epic), and for each genre, we compute the number of complements offered. We have to drop games for which we do not have information about the month of release. Additionally, to ensure consistent classification of games, we rely on the genre indicated on Moby Games, rather than the genre declared on each platform. We obtained, in total, 8889 games on Steam and 660 games on Epic over the period. Given the variety of genres and combination of genres, we keep the 20 main genres (which represent about 88% of games) and group the remaining genres in the “Other” genre group.

We compute, for each platform p, genre g, and month t, the number of games active on the platform and denote it Gamespgt. This captures the level of within-platform competition in each genre over time. To compare competition intensity across platforms and genres, we then compute a standardized score (Z-score) for each Gamespgt, which reflects how a given genre is positioned relative to the distribution of all genres on the same platform. This allows us to assess whether a particular genre is relatively crowded (or sparse) on a given platform at a given point

in time. This score is computed as follows: Zpgt = Gamespgt −Gamespt

SD Gamespt ð Þ . Figure A3 displays the Z-scores

for selected genres across both platforms, aggregated over the entire observation period.

A Z-score of 3, for example, indicates that the genre is significantly more populated than the average genre on that platform, suggesting a high level of within-platform competition.

We then compute, for each genre and month, a ratio that captures the difference in Z-scores between the two platforms—where s denotes Steam and e denotes Epic. This ratio measures the relative attractiveness of a genre in terms of competition intensity across platforms. It is calculated as follows: Ratiogt = Zsgt

Zegt. If the ratio is close to zero, it indicates that the two platforms are relatively similar in terms of the number of competitors in a given genre. A large positive value suggests that the genre is significantly less crowded on Epic than on Steam, making Epic potentially more attractive for complementors in that genre. Conversely, a negative value indicates that Epic is more crowded than Steam for that genre, reducing its relative attractiveness in terms of competitive intensity. The values of these ratios are aggregated over the entire observation period and subsequently denoted Ratiog.

Figure A4 illustrates how this measure varies across genres. We include Ratiog as an additional regressor in our multihoming regressions to account for the relative attractiveness of genre-level competition across platforms.

A.9 | Robustness check: Intensity of multihoming at the publisher level

The main analyses of multihoming in the paper are conducted at the game level. As some publishers release multiple games, we complement our approach by studying multihoming intensity at the publisher level. To do so, we construct a new dataset comprising the subsample of 4821 games (out of our original 8101) for which publisher information is available, covering 2400 unique publishers. The distribution of games per publisher is highly skewed: 72.6% have only one game, 13.3% have two, and 4.8% have three. The remaining 7.1% manage between four and 56 games.

For each publisher, we calculate a multihoming intensity measure defined as the share of their games available on both platforms, as of June 2022. This measure ranges from 0 (none of the publisher's games multihome) to 1 (all games multihome). We then regress this intensity on the average characteristics of the games in each publisher's portfolio—specifically, the share of Indie games and the share of multiplayer games—alongside controls such as the total number of games in the portfolio and variables from our main model. Due to missing values on some controls (in particular for development team size), the effective sample size is reduced to 1568 publishers. On average, 69% of games in a publisher's portfolio are Indie, and 35% are multiplayer.

Table A9 presents the results from OLS regressions. Column 1 uses the full sample; Columns 2 and 3 restrict the sample to publishers with more than one and more than five games, respectively. While the results broadly align with our game-level findings—the positive impact

However, in this section, we aim to provide evidence that the complementor groups we study did not differ significantly before the shock. To do so, we will proceed in two steps. First, we compute average participation, at the sale level, for each group of complementors and present these results in Figure B2. As a second step, we estimate a model structurally equivalent to our main sales regressions but restricted to the pre-shock period. In this setting, the complementor-type indicators (Indie and multiplayer) enter the model without interaction terms, as there is no post-period. Because game fixed effects are collinear with these time-invariant indicators, we instead control for all variables used in our multihoming regressions, including both time-varying and invariant covariates. We further include sale fixed effects to capture time-specific shocks. Figure B3 presents the resulting coefficients. The lack of statistically significant differences supports our identification strategy by indicating that our groups of interest did not differ systematically in their sales participation before the shock.

B.4 | Additional analysis: Minor versus major sales

In this additional analysis, we explore potential heterogeneity in complementors’ responses across different types of sales. As pointed out earlier, and shown in Table B1, sales events vary considerably in their popularity—some, such as the Winter Sales, attract broad participation, while others are more niche and appeal to specific game types. We, therefore, re-estimate our main models using a split sample approach. We classify a sale as major if at least 40% of games in our sample participate, and as minor otherwise. We use matched samples for these estimations (as in Models 5–7 of Table 4). We find that the responses to EGS's launch seem to be entirely driven by minor sales: Indie games become significantly less likely to participate in minor sales after the entry, while multiplayer games are significantly more likely to do so. For major sales, we observe no significant changes for either group. These results add nuance to the overall picture: evidently, game developers are not willing to forego the high-demand periods generated by major sales. Instead, they react in terms of their responsiveness to more targeted promotional events. This also puts into perspective our prior assessment of the economic significance of the effects. The average game participates in only around 5%–6% of minor sales. As a result, the estimated coefficients for Indie (Model 2, β= −0:027) and multiplayer games (Model 4, β=0:030) imply large economic effect sizes (Table B3).

B.5 | Additional analysis: Discounts outside sales

We analyze how EGS's launch affected complementors’ tendency to offer their product at a discount outside Steam's sale promotions. Part of the aim of our study is to show how increased platform competition impacts their responsiveness to orchestration attempts. However, it is possible that complementors generally have less of an incentive to discount their product, which could then offer an alternative explanation for our results. However, if this is the case, then we would also observe a change in their tendency to do so outside Steam sales. To test this, we estimate a series of regressions using a game-week panel that excludes weeks with an active Steam sale. As in our main analysis, we use models with time-varying controls as well as matched samples. Results are presented in Table B4. Across all models, we find no significant effect of EGS's launch on the likelihood of games being discounted outside of promotional periods. We interpret this as evidence that complementors are indeed responding specifically to platform orchestration efforts rather than changing their overall discounting behavior.

B.6 | Additional analysis: Interaction between games characteristics

Complementor types are not mutually exclusive. For example, an Indie game may include multiplayer functionality. To further explore how these two dimensions interact and which of the opposing effects dominates, we conduct an additional set of regressions. We define four groups

For instance, the effect for “Indie- singleplayer” games becomes statistically insignificant. Nonetheless, the overall pattern of results reinforces our theoretical predictions: complementors’ responses to the entry of a rival platform depend on the interplay between their resource endowment and their reliance on network effects.

B.7 | Additional analysis: Interdependence between decisions—Does multihoming determine sales participation?

It is possible that the decisions to multihome and to continue participating in Steam sales are interdependent. We already explore this question to some extent in Appendix A (Additional analysis: Interdependence of decisions—Does sales participation determine multihoming?), where we re-estimate part of our multihoming analyses including the intensity of sales participation as an additional regressor. There, we find no significant effect. In this section, we investigate the reverse relationship: whether participation in sales is influenced by the decision to multihome. Indeed, multihoming games may be more or less likely to adjust their responsiveness to the incumbent's orchestration attempts. To test this possibility, we run an additional set of regressions in which we let the probability of sales participation vary between games that multihome and those that do not. We further analyze how this relationship differs across complementor types.

Instrumental variable approach: Estimating the influence of multihoming presents an endogeneity concern. Since both homing decision and sales participation can be seen as manifestations of a complementor's ongoing engagement with (or support for) the incumbent platform, the error term in a regression of sales participation is likely correlated with the multihoming indicator. To address this issue, we use an instrumental variables approach. Specifically, we instrument the multihoming indicator (the endogenous regressor here) with a dummy

indicating whether the game was developed with Epic's Unreal Engine.68 In our main analyses, we found that the use of Unreal Engine (which serves as a control there) is predictive of multihoming.69 In a separate regression, we found that Unreal Engine use is not related to a change in complementors’ likelihood to participate in sales promotions due to the entry. Hence, we consider it a valid instrument for the purpose of the additional analysis described here. Furthermore, in line with our main specification, we apply coarsened exact matching (CEM) to reduce observable imbalance across game types. Combined with our instrumental variables approach, which addresses potential endogeneity in the multihoming indicator, this ensures greater validity of the estimated effects.

Table B6 reports the results. Models 1 to 3 are estimated using OLS and do not account for potential endogeneity in the multihoming indicator. However, they are based on matched samples (CEM) to ensure a good comparability between indie and non-indie games, and between multiplayer and singleplayer games. Models 5 to 7 are estimated via Two- Stage Least Squares (2SLS). Model 4 reports the first stage. To analyze variation between complementor types, we enter a triple-interaction with an Indie dummy in Models 2 and 6, and a multiplayer dummy in Models 3 and 7. Across specifications and estimation approaches, we find no evidence that sales participation differs systematically between multihoming and singlehoming games, nor that this relationship varies by complementor type.

As an alternative approach, we restrict the sample to multihoming games and reestimate our main model. Specifically, in Models 8 and 9 of Table B6, we limit the analysis to those games that are observed on both platforms and re-run our main specification separately for indie and multiplayer games. Naturally, this leads to a considerably smaller sample size. While statistically insignificant, we still find a negative effect of the entry for indie games (consistent with prior findings and expectations). For multihoming games, we find a positive effect (p<0:1). This indicates that multiplayer games continue to participate in sales, even when they multihome. Admittedly, this is a somewhat unexpected result. On the one hand, our prediction is that multiplayer games have weaker incentives to multihome, but stronger incentives to participate in sales after an entry, as their individual interest in platform size aligns with the collective interest in the incumbent's ecosystem. On the other hand, once multiplayer games do multihome, it is less clear what the prediction should be regarding their engagement in orchestration efforts by the incumbent. A potential explanation is that this type of complementor has been attracted to EGS through unobserved incentives. It is not uncommon in the video game industry that platform owners pay complementors to join their platform (Cennamo & Santalo, 2013, cf.), and such arrangements are typically not observable to researchers. If these incentives are strong enough, they may lead a multiplayer game to join the entrant while still maintaining active engagement with the incumbent's ecosystem to preserve access to its larger user base. In this light, the observed behavior remains consistent with our theoretical expectations. The lower statistical precision of the estimates likely reflects the fact that this is a boundary case with less clearly defined strategic motivations.

B.8 | Additional analysis: The role of pre-EGS review count and score

In our theoretical framework, we argue that complementors’ resource endowment influences their continued participation in sales promotions. Empirically, we capture variation in resource endowment via a binary variable indicating whether a game is categorized as Indie (as opposed to “Triple-A” games). The underlying argument is that these games, given their limited resources, are less able to compete effectively in the incumbent's ecosystem. To provide further evidence supporting this mechanism, we now analyze how the entry affects the behavior of games that are more popular or of higher popularity—two attributes that likely “signal” a stronger position within the incumbent ecosystem, as these games have either succeeded in this environment already (e.g., excellent user reception) or offer a superior value proposition. We use review counts as a proxy for sales, and user review scores as a proxy for quality. To identify highly popular games, we create a binary variable that indicates whether a game belongs to the top quartile in terms of user review counts at the time of EGS's launch. Similarly, we identify high-quality games with a binary variable coded as one if the game belongs to the top quartile in terms of user review scores. We then re-estimate our main model. Models 1–3 use the full sample without matching, while Models 4 and 5 apply coarsened exact matching on control variables. Results are presented in Table B7. We find that both high-popularity and high-quality games are more likely to participate in sales promotions after the rival platform's entry, compared to those of lower popularity or quality. This is consistent with our theoretical expectation that complementors better positioned to thrive in the incumbent ecosystem are more inclined to continue supporting its orchestration efforts.

This appendix provides additional descriptive statistics on the two platforms under study, including their composition in terms of prices, genres, and user demographics, as well as supplementary analyses on the impact of the entrant's arrival on pricing and user numbers.

C.2 | Additional descriptive statistics: Differentiation of platforms

The total sample consists of 11,439 games, of which 9335 are only observed on Steam, 1458 only on EGS, and 645 on both platforms as of June 2022. When possible, we compare the characteristics of games available on Steam, EGS, and on both platforms to assess the degree of product differentiation across the two competing platforms.

Prices: Table C1 presents summary statistics for list and current prices across both platforms. List prices refer to the non-discounted price of a game. While these may evolve over time, they tend to be more stable than current prices, which are frequently adjusted, particularly during platform-wide sales promotions. On average, list prices are lower on Steam (15.50 USD) than on EGS (19.82 USD). A similar pattern holds for current prices, which include temporary discounts.

Figure C4 illustrates the price distributions across platforms, highlighting that games on EGS tend to be priced higher. Interestingly, the price distribution of multihoming games—those available on both platforms—closely resembles that of games exclusive to each individual platform.

Type of games: The composition of the two platforms’ catalogs also differs along several nonprice dimensions, as illustrated in Figure C5. For example, the incumbent platform Steam features a much higher share of “Indie” games compared to EGS. Steam's catalog also includes a significantly larger proportion of multiplayer games (29.6%) relative to EGS (4.1%). In terms of development team size, Steam is dominated by games created by very small teams (66% of titles are developed by teams of just one to three people). Genre composition varies as well: Steam has a strong emphasis on Adventure games (accounting for around 53% of its catalog), while EGS leans more heavily toward Action titles (38%). However, there are two important limitations to these comparisons. First, while we observe a substantial portion of EGS's catalog, our Steam sample is restricted to its most popular titles and therefore does not reflect the platform's full offering. Second, the two platforms differ in terms of maturity. Rietveld and Eggers (2018) emphasize that platform age shapes demand heterogeneity over the life cycle (e.g., in consumers’ willingness to pay and interest in novelty), which in turn affects complementors’ success and profitability. This may explain why the platforms appear quite different despite offering comparable services, such as user interfaces, features that support network effects, and regular sales promotions.

Consumer side: To comment on the heterogeneity of users affiliated with both platforms, we collect data from the web-audience tracking tool Similarweb, which provides information on the web traffic of major websites, in particular the socio-demographics of their audiences (age and gender). In our context, these are Steampowered.com and Epicgames.com. While the observation period (January to March 2024) is more recent than the timeframe analyzed in the main body of the paper, we believe the statistics remain informative. Figure C6 summarizes the demographic composition of the two audiences. Overall, the differences are minimal, suggesting that the platforms attract broadly similar user bases in terms of age and gender.

Our dataset, crawled from the website steamdb.info, provides game-day level information on both list and discounted prices. We exploit this data to estimate a model similar to the one we

estimated for sales, using prices as a dependent variable and interactions between our variables of interest (indie, multiplayer) with an indicator for the post-entry time period. The goal is to assess whether the pricing of games on Steam changed following the entry of EGS. While list prices reflect long-term pricing strategies (typically adjusted infrequently), current prices are subject to short-term “strategy” and are often influenced by sales participation. We restrict the sample to the same 24-month window used in our sales analysis, covering the 12 months before and after the entry. The final sample consists of 108,107 observations on 5536 games. These regressions all include a measure for the age of the game, as prices tend to “naturally” decrease over the life cycle of games. The results, presented in Table C2, suggest that the current prices remain largely unaffected by the entry, while the list prices are affected. In particular, we observe that multiplayer games tend to be less expensive, ceteris paribus, after the shock, while indie games tend to be more expensive. Overall, these findings indicate that, in addition to adjustments in sales participation, complementors’ longterm pricing strategies responded to the platform entry. Moreover, the heterogeneity of these effects aligns with our theoretical expectations: complementors with strong incentives to preserve the existing ecosystem (e.g., multiplayer games reliant on network effects) appear to lower their list prices in an effort to boost demand. In contrast, those that view the entrant as a viable alternative (e.g., Indie developers) do not exhibit such behavior—in fact, they tend to raise their list prices, all else equal.

APPENDIX D: ADDITIONAL DISCUSSION

D.1 | How the “cross-play” functionality could affect our study In this section, we offer a discussion of recent developments in cross-play functionality and how they relate to the mechanisms studied in our paper. The arguments we developed rest on the assumption that network effects are platform-specific—that is, consumers can only play games together if they are on the same platform. For example, Steam users can only play with other Steam users, or in the home console space, PlayStation owners with other PlayStation owners. This form of incompatibility has been a common practice in the video game industry.

Recent trends toward so-called cross-play functionality are driving a push toward interoperability among user bases. This implies that complement-level network effects have begun to operate across platform boundaries—in other words, network effects are becoming increasingly game-specific rather than platform-specific. This shift has met resistance from some console manufacturers. Most notably, Sony initially blocked cross-play entirely, later imposed charges on developers who sought to enable it, and ultimately permitted it for some games after Epic Games’ Fortnite became the most-played game on PlayStation (Partis, 2021; Warren, 2021). This highlights the reluctance of platform owners to embrace interoperability, as doing so may undermine their market power and control over user interactions (Morton et al., 2023). In addition, Sony only allowed it after one specific complementor—Epic Games—gained sufficient influence to challenge the platform's governance stance. Generally, platform owners may deliberately restrict interoperability for strategic reasons. Sony's resistance to cross-play in the video game console market is a good example. Conversely, smaller entrants might want to promote interoperability to erode the market power of incumbents.

In our empirical setting, Epic Games’ strategy illustrates this dynamic. In June 2022, it launched a cross-play tool designed to simplify cross-platform integration for game developers (Epic Online Services, 2022). This move underscores two important points: (i) implementing cross-play remains a significant technical challenge for developers, and (ii) Epic Games had strategic incentives to reduce the platform-specificity of network effects and thereby challenge Steam's dominant position. In addition to the June 2022 toolkit, Epic Games made cross-play a requirement for multiplayer titles distributed through its store in September 2024 (Benfell, 2024). However, these developments fall outside the temporal scope of our empirical analysis, as our sample ends prior to the release of these tools.

To assess whether early instances of crossplay functionality might already be present in our data—and thus potentially affect our findings—we collected information on crossplay-enabled games using a curated Wikipedia list.70 Only 11 games in our sample support crossplay, suggesting that, indeed, it was not yet common during the period we analyze.71 This supports the view that multiplayer games in our setting continued to rely on Steam's installed base advantage. Accordingly, the setting we study is still characterized by a lack of interoperability between platforms.

70https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_that_support_cross-platform_play. 71Note that the small number of crossplay-enabled games prevents a proper econometric analysis of this subsample.
